newsitem.title: INDIA: PRESS DIGEST - Indian newspapers - January 18.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Indian newspapers - January 18.

text.p: Following is a summary of major Indian business and political stories in leading newspapers prepared for REUTERS by Business News and Information Services Pvt Ltd, New Delhi Tel:3326806, 3326813, 3326849 Fax:+91-11-3351006 E-mail: biznis@giasdl01.vsnl.net.in.
Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
TOP STORIES
The Hindustan Times
FOUR DETAINED IN TRADE UNIONIST MURDER CASE

The Bombay police detained four suspects for interrogation in connection with the killing of trade union leader Datta Samant. The police expected crucial information on the identity of the murderers from Samant's driver, who was injured in the shootout and was still not out of danger.

Maharashtra home minister Gopinath Munde said the police expected a breakthrough in the case. Bombay observed a partial bandh to protest against the killing of the trade union leader. But the police said there were no reports of untoward incidents from any part of the city.
Indian Express
PRIMIER TRIES TO PLEASE COALITION PARTNERS
The Steering Committee meeting of the United Front (UF) saw Prime Minister Deve Gowda bending forward to keep the partners in the multi-party coalition in good humour.
Union Minister C M Ibrahim kept away from the meeting, apparently to sooth the hurt sentiments of Defence Minister Mulayam Singh Yadav and the Left parties.

In view of the unity moves initiated by Congress chief Sitaram Kesri which may lead to the UF's fall, Gowda's strategy has been one of balancing the various mutually opposed factions of the UF to keep the government going.
The Economic Times
PUBLIC OFFER MUST FOR ACQUISITIONS UP TO 75 PCT
The Justice PN Bhagwati Committee on corporate takeovers decided that a public offer would be made mandatory for acquisitions upto 75 percent stake in a company.

Currently, this offer is required to be made for acquisitions upto 50 percent, and not beyond. An acquirer, however, could increase his stake by two percent every year up to 75 percent without having to make a public offer, the committee suggested. Sources said this change in the public offer norms was expected to make acquisitions more transparent as also to protect the interests of small shareholders.
NEW CIVIL AVIATION POLICY IN A FORTNIGHT
Civil Aviation Minister C M Ibrahim hinted at declaration of the new civil aviation policy within 15 days, adding that the policy had already been submitted to the cabinet.
The minister reiterated foreign airlines would not be allowed to invest in domestic carriers, and said Jet Airways would have to dilute its foreign equity.
Ibrahim said he had reservations about foreign investment in the airlines, but welcomed foreign investment in the aviation infrastructure sector.
FRESH CONCESSIONS FOR FOREIGN INVESTMENTS
The finance ministry may grant fresh concessions to further encourage foreign institutional investment (FII) in Indian debt.

A decision on removal of withholding tax on interest earned by FIIs on Indian debt was likely soon, said sources. The government is understandably planning to allow FIIs to subscribe to government securities.
FIIs have been keen on subscribing to government securities as they are zero risk and can be more easily sold in the market.
Giving a boost to FII investment in debt is part of the overall capital market reforms package being worked out by the government. These may form a part of the budget announcements.
Financial Express
INFRASTRUCTURE FINANCE COMPANY GOES ON STREAM

The government announced the incorporation of the Infrastructure Development Finance Company (IDFC) under the Companies Act with a token capital of 20 million rupees on January 31, 1997. The authorised capital would be raised to 10 billion rupees by 1997/98 (April-March).

Domestic financial institutions made in principle commitment to subscribe to the equity capital of IDFC to the extent of 3.25 billion rupees. Foreign investors committed to invest $100 million in IDFC while the World Bank agreed to be a lender.
IDFC will finance commercially viable infrastructure sector projects including power, railways, telecommunication systems, roads, highways and urban services.
RELIANCE SEEKS STAY ON SUSPENSION ORDER

Reliance Consultancy Services (RCS), Reliance Industries' share transfer agent, has sought a stay on the stock market regulator SEBI's order to suspend operations from February 1, 1997 for six months.

The stay was sought till the finance ministry cleared the RCS appeal challenging the order. RCS, while challenging the order, had contended it would cause problems for investors as it would not be able to complete the pending cases within the allotted period. SEBI had given RCS time till January 31, 1997 to make alternate arrangements.
Business Standard
BPL CELLULAR PLANS PRIVATE PLACEMENT OF ADRS

BPL Cellular Holdings Ltd (BPLCHL) plans to make a private placement of American Depositary Receipts (ADRs) to raise around $80 million. It has short-listed two international investors and a deal is likely to be reached soon, sources said.

Earlier, BPL Cellular had withdrawn its proposed $215 million ADR flotation after investors demanded a hefty discount on the initial offer price. BPLCHL hopes to complete the private placement within three weeks.
The company has set a band of $8-11 per ADR to provide Morgan Stanley, the adviser to the issue, enough flexibility in pricing the issue.
PREMIER AUTOMOBILE, PEUGEOT TIES UNDER STRAIN

The alliance between Premier Automobiles (PAL) and Peugeot may be heading for a split over the issue of capitalisation of losses incurred by PAL-Peugeot in fiscal 1996/97 (April-March) due to the labour dispute at the Kalyan plant.

Even as Peugeot is pushing for capitalisation of the losses, PAL says the move will not solve the company's problems. Due to labour strife in 1996, PAL had failed to invest fresh funds in the joint venture (JV) to offset the company's losses.

Capitalisation of losses would present an unrealistic picture of the company's financial health, claimed PAL sources. PAL was also opposing Peugeot's attempt to pump in fresh funds into the JV to raise its stake, said sources.
BOURSE REGULATOR AIMS TO TIGHTEN SURVEILLANCE
Stock exchanges (SEs) across the country would come under a more streamlined surveillance mechanism being put in place by the stock market regulator, SEBI.

The streamlined surveillance would relate to the imposition of price bands, making it mandatory for SEs to implement price bands uniformly based on the previous day's closing price of the stock. At present, price bands on some exchanges are based on the opening price of stocks on the same trading day.
SEBI will also probe the wild price volatility witnessed on the SEs in the past three days.
HOECHST PHARMA ARM SHELVES EXPANSION
Hoechst Marion Roussel (HMR), the pharmaceutical arm of the $36 billion Hoechst group, has suspended its expansion plans, citing delays in enactment of a new patent legislation.

Though the German parent desired to invest in India's pharmaceutical operations, existing patent laws made it difficult for foreign companies to operate and invest in research and development, company sources said.
Despite the lack of stronger patent laws, the company is going ahead with new launches with a view to increase market share. Hoechst now holds 3.7 percent of the domestic market and is ranked fourth.
PARTIAL PRIVATISATION OF RAILWAYS ON CARDS

The Parliamentary Committee on railway convention is considering partial privatisation of the utility to increase its profitability. The committee hopes to submit its interim report before the railway budget is finalised.

The committee is currently studying the operations of three zonal railways: Eastern Railway, South-Eastern Railway and Metro Railway. Given the decline in budgetary support, the railways are under strain to finance their development projects.
The privatisation exercise is said to be prompted by the fact that the railways were finding it difficult to borrow from the market.
The Observer of Business and Politics
BOMBAY BOURSE SHEDS 30 POINTS
The stock market continued to fluctuate wildly. However, despite continuation of speculative activity, there was no panic as seen the previous day.

The Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) sensitive index closed at 3422.35 points, after touching an intra-day high of 3480.98, netting a loss of 30 points. Most of the operators squared up their outstanding positions because of the last day of the settlement on BSE.
SUGAR PRICE HIKE BEFORE BUGDET

Finance Minister P Chidambaram said levy sugar prices would be raised before the budget for fiscal 1997/98 (April-March). He said the hike in petrogoods' prices would, however, come after the presentation of the budget.

Stating this at the United Front steering committee meeting, the Finance Minister said the government would be forced to take these measures in order to make up the huge deficits. He also disclosed that the deficit on the oil pool account would increase by 170 billion rupees while the subsidy on the levy sugar account would go up to 12.88 billion rupees by March.
ROYAL & SUN SEEKS MAJORITY STAKE

British insurance major Royal & Sun Alliance is demanding a majority equity stake as a precondition for its tie-up with DCM Shriram Consolidated. The two firms had signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) in 1993, anticipating the liberalisation of the insurance sector.

The only condition finalised between the two firms in the MoU is that the UK group will not ally with any other Indian company in the insurance sector. The insurance regulatory authority, however, has yet to lay down ground rules for private participation and equity holding norms in the sector.
SHARP DIP IN PERFORMANCE OF INFRASTRUCTURE UNITS
A sharp fall in the growth of infrastructure industries led to the slack in industrial growth during the first eight months of the current fiscal (April-March).

A select group of 24 industries recorded a mere five percent growth (11 percent) during the period. Cumulative growth in the infrastructure sector, having about 29 percent weightage in the index of industrial production, fell to 3.3 percent during April- November 1996 (9.3 percent).

Seven industries, including crude petroleum, fertiliser, cloth and jute recorded negative growth. The electricity sector grew at 3.2 percent (9.9 percent). Better performance was recorded by the sugar, cars, motor cycle and three-wheeler sectors which grew at 37.6 percent, 21 percent, 18 percent and 33.9 percent, respectively.
Business Line
HYDEL POWER PACKAGE SOON
The government will soon formulate a national policy on hydro-electric (hydel) power development.

Power minister S Venugopalachari said the policy would be aimed at correcting the growing imbalance in the thermal-hydel power mix and fuller exploitation of the 84,000 MW potential of which only 15 percent had been developed.

He said against an ideal thermal-hydel mix of 60:40, the ratio stood at 75:25 in 1995/96 (April-March). To arrest this trend, the minister said the new policy would include, among other things, incentives for development of mega hydel projects at suitable locations both by the public and private sectors.
